newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians protest again but no sign of bailout.
newsitem.headline: Albanians protest again but no sign of bailout.

text.p: Thousands of Albanian protesters marched for a 13th day on Monday to demand that the government pay compensation for the collapse of popular but fraudulent investment schemes.
"Down with the government", "We want our money back," a demonstration by some 3,000 people chanted in this southern Albania port.
They carried pictures of a protester who died last week during clashes with riot police.
Protests and rioting have swept Europe's poorest country since last month when five pyramid schemes collapsed, wiping out the life savings of many Albanians.
Protests have been calmer in Vlore and Fier, to the north, since authorities withdrew riot police over the weekend and let the marches proceed.
But police in the capital of Tirana have kept a close eye out for anyone trying to start a demonstration and they have broken up any gatherings quickly.

In Vlore, which has been the centre of protests in recent days, the National Commercial Bank opened for the first time in 10 days to distribute some of the frozen assets of the failed pyramid schemes.
About 50 people lined up outside the bank. One older woman showed a deposit certificate for 40,000 leks (about $400) and said she would receive 52 percent of that.
"It's better than nothing," she told reporters.

The government seized about $300 million in assets from two failed schemes last month and said it would distrubute them to clients, but the government has refused to pay any compensation from state coffers.
Attention is now focused on four other funds, which insist they are genuine business concerns, but have frozen customers' capital and cut interest payments sharply.
The head of one of the largest companies, Vehbi Alimucaj of Vefa, appeared on television on Sunday to assure investors that their money was safe.

Vefa's name is everywhere in Albania, from supermarkets and apartments to a large neon sign in Tirana's central square. But it has frozen deposits and is paying interest only at a greatly reduced rate.
More than 100 people waited outside Vefa offices in Tirana on Monday.
Albania's right-wing government has called for talks with the opposition socialists this week to defuse a crisis and stop the violence which has swept the country.
Ruined investors blamed the right-wing government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi for failing to warn them about the risk and for letting the unregulated companies flourish.
The ruling Democrats acknowledged hundreds of thousands of Albanians lost large sums of money when get-rich-schemes went bust in January.
Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu, also the leader of the Democratic Party, called on socialist leader Rexhep Majdani to meet him on Wednesday.
The socialists, the ex-Communist Party, have boycotted parliament since general elections last year which they said were fraudulent.
They have also refused to take part in talks on the failed schemes, which are estimated to have held $1 to $2 billion in assets and paid interest of up to 60 percent a month before they collapsed.
